reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording

summary.text: For a typical customer, the model gives a clearly higher predicted chance that a customer leaves if the customer has an international plan (about 79%) than if the customer has no international plan (about 23%).

For a typical customer, the model gives a higher predicted chance that a customer leaves if the customer is in Washington (about 46%) than if state is something other than Alabama, Hawaii, Idaho, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Arkansas, Maine, Minnesota, Missouri, Mississippi, Montana, North Dakota, Nebraska, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oklahoma, California, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, Connecticut, Florida (about 23%) (on the training data only).

For a typical customer, the model gives a clearly lower predicted chance that a customer leaves if the customer has a voice-mail plan (about 3%) than if the customer has no voice-mail plan (about 23%).

Through one part of the model, the customer-service calls only clearly adds to the predicted chance that a customer leaves from 3 calls upwards: for a typical such customer, going from 0 calls to 4 calls moves it from about 23% to about 77%.

A higher total evening charge clearly raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves, but only if total daytime minutes is above 180 minutes: for a typical customer, total evening charge going from 11.76 US dollars to 22.57 US dollars moves the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 23% to about 55% if total daytime minutes is above 180 minutes, and from about 23% to about 23% if total daytime minutes is at or below 180 minutes.
The model ignores account length, area code, total daytime calls, total international calls, total international minutes and total night-time minutes.
